fungal.summary: A fungal leaf disease. Most fungal diseases spread faster in warm, humid, crowded canopies.
act_now: Remove and destroy the most affected leaves away from the field.
Avoid working in the crop while leaves are wet; you spread spores.
Increase spacing or prune to improve airflow and sunlight penetration.
organic: Spray neem extract or a copper-based product approved for this crop, following the label.
Apply compost tea or a silicon amendment only where locally recommended.
chemical: If disease pressure is high, use a fungicide registered for this crop and disease.
Rotate active ingredients between sprays to slow resistance; never exceed label rates.
prevent: Rotate with a non-host crop for at least one season.
Use certified, disease-free seed and resistant varieties where available.
Mulch to stop soil splash and water at the base, not overhead.
fungal.escalate: If more than 30% of the canopy is affected, or it is spreading fast after 5-7 days, contact your local extension officer.

bacterial.summary: A bacterial disease. It spreads through splashing water, contaminated tools, and infected seed.
act_now: Remove infected plants or leaves and destroy them; do not compost.
Disinfect pruning tools with alcohol or bleach solution between plants.
Stop overhead irrigation and avoid moving through wet plants.
organic: Copper-based sprays approved for the crop can slow spread; follow the label.
Improve drainage and airflow; avoid high-nitrogen fertilizer flushes.
chemical: There is no cure once a plant is infected. Protect healthy plants with a registered copper bactericide if locally recommended.
Antibiotic sprays are restricted in many countries; check local rules first.
prevent: Use clean, certified seed and rotate crops.
Remove crop debris after harvest and control volunteer plants.
Avoid overhead watering and keep tools clean.
bacterial.escalate: If new plants keep showing symptoms after removal, contact your extension officer to confirm the diagnosis.

viral.summary: A viral disease. There is no chemical cure; management focuses on the vector and on stopping spread.
act_now: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately, including roots.
Control the insect vector (whitefly, aphid, thrips) with traps and approved products.
Wash hands and tools after handling infected plants.
organic: Use yellow sticky traps and row covers where practical.
Spray neem or insecticidal soap for vector control, following the label.
chemical: Use a registered insecticide for the vector, not the virus; rotate modes of action.
Do not expect a spray to cure plants that are already infected.
prevent: Plant resistant or tolerant varieties where available.
Use clean seed and transplants; isolate new seedlings.
Control weeds that host the vector around the field.
viral.escalate: If more than 10% of plants are infected, or the vector population is high, contact your extension officer before replanting.

pest.summary: A pest infestation. Check the underside of leaves and look for webbing, stippling, or insects.
act_now: Inspect several plants across the field to estimate the infestation level.
Remove heavily infested leaves and destroy them.
Reduce water stress; stressed plants suffer more damage.
organic: Spray water or insecticidal soap on the undersides of leaves.
Encourage predators such as ladybirds and predatory mites; avoid broad-spectrum sprays.
chemical: Use a miticide or insecticide registered for this pest and crop only if thresholds are exceeded.
Rotate active ingredients; spider mites develop resistance quickly.
prevent: Rotate crops and remove crop residues.
Keep field edges weed-free; monitor weekly with sticky traps.
Avoid dusty conditions and over-fertilizing with nitrogen.
pest.escalate: If webbing covers growing tips or plants are defoliating, contact your extension officer.

healthy.summary: The leaf looks healthy. Keep scouting so problems are caught early.
act_now: Check the underside of leaves and new growth weekly.
Take photos of any new spots and compare them over time.
organic: Maintain compost and mulch to build soil health.
Keep beneficial insect habitat around the field.
chemical: No spray is needed for a healthy leaf.
Avoid preventive spraying; it wastes money and can cause resistance.
prevent: Rotate crops and use resistant varieties.
Water at the base in the morning so leaves dry before night.
Space plants for airflow and remove crop debris after harvest.
healthy.escalate: If symptoms appear later, take a clear photo and ask again.

maize_common_rust.summary: Common rust shows orange-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces. It is favoured by cool, humid nights and usually causes limited loss unless it appears early and spreads fast.
act_now: Check the upper leaves of 10 plants across the field.
Record how many plants show pustules; rust usually does not need spraying.
Keep the crop healthy; drought stress makes rust worse.
organic: Sulphur or neem products can slow rust if applied early, following the label.
Plant resistant hybrids next season.
chemical: Spray a registered triazole or strobilurin fungicide only if rust appears before tasselling and is spreading.
One well-timed spray is usually better than repeated spraying.
prevent: Avoid late planting and excessive nitrogen.
Remove volunteer maize that carries the fungus between seasons.
maize_common_rust.escalate: If rust appears before tasselling and more than 20% of leaf area is affected, consult an extension officer about a fungicide.

maize_northern_leaf_blight.summary: Northern leaf blight causes long, cigar-shaped grey-green lesions. It survives on crop residue and spreads in humid weather.
act_now: Remove or bury crop residue after harvest.
Avoid overhead irrigation and improve airflow.
Check lower leaves first; the disease moves upward.
organic: Neem or copper sprays may slow spread; apply before lesions are widespread.
Use compost to support plant vigour.
chemical: A registered fungicide at first lesions can protect yield in susceptible hybrids.
Do not spray after the crop has reached dough stage.
prevent: Plant resistant hybrids and rotate with legumes.
Avoid continuous maize on the same plot.
maize_northern_leaf_blight.escalate: If lesions reach the ear leaf before flowering, contact an extension officer.

maize_cercospora_and_gray_leaf_spot.summary: Gray leaf spot causes rectangular grey lesions between veins. It builds up in fields with continuous maize and surface residue.
act_now: Improve airflow and avoid working in wet foliage.
Remove infected residue after harvest.
Check whether the variety is known to be susceptible.
organic: Neem or copper products can slow spread early in the season.
Mulch with clean material to reduce splash.
chemical: Use a registered fungicide if lesions reach the ear leaf and weather stays humid.
Rotate active ingredients.
prevent: Rotate with soybean or another non-host.
Use resistant varieties and clean seed.
maize_cercospora_and_gray_leaf_spot.escalate: If the ear leaf is affected before flowering, get a second opinion before spraying.

tomato_late_blight.summary: Late blight causes water-soaked lesions with white mould on the underside. It can destroy a field in days in cool, wet weather.
act_now: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately; do not compost.
Harvest healthy fruit early if the disease is close.
Stop overhead irrigation and improve ventilation.
organic: Copper-based sprays can protect healthy plants; apply before infection.
Remove volunteers and nightshade weeds that host the pathogen.
chemical: Use a registered late-blight fungicide preventively when weather is cool and wet.
Alternate active ingredients to slow resistance.
prevent: Plant certified seed and resistant varieties.
Avoid overhead watering and dense planting.
Do not store infected tubers or fruit with healthy ones.
tomato_late_blight.escalate: Act the same day: late blight spreads explosively. If you see white mould on lesions, contact an extension officer immediately.

potato_late_blight.summary: Late blight on potato causes dark water-soaked leaf lesions and white mould. It can rot tubers in storage.
act_now: Remove and destroy infected foliage; do not compost.
Stop overhead irrigation and harvest tubers only after foliage dies down.
Check stored tubers for rot.
organic: Copper protectant sprays before infection.
Remove volunteer potatoes and infected debris.
chemical: Preventive registered fungicides are far more effective than curative sprays.
Follow local late-blight forecasting alerts.
prevent: Use certified seed potatoes and resistant varieties.
Rotate away from potatoes and tomatoes for 2-3 seasons.
Earth up tubers well to reduce spore wash into soil.
potato_late_blight.escalate: If lesions appear and weather is cool and wet, treat within 24 hours and alert neighbouring farmers.

potato_early_blight.summary: Early blight causes brown concentric rings on older leaves. It usually starts on lower leaves and moves upward.
act_now: Remove affected lower leaves and improve airflow.
Keep plants well fed and watered; stressed plants get hit harder.
Mulch to prevent soil splash.
organic: Neem or copper sprays can slow progress.
Compost tea may support plant health but is not a cure.
chemical: Use a registered fungicide if lesions are moving up the canopy.
Rotate with a different mode of action next spray.
prevent: Use certified seed and resistant varieties.
potato_early_blight.escalate: If more than 30% of leaves are affected, consult an extension officer.

tomato_bacterial_spot.summary: Bacterial spot causes small dark greasy spots on leaves and fruit. It spreads in rain splash and on contaminated seed.
act_now: Remove infected leaves and fruit; disinfect tools between plants.
Avoid overhead watering and working in wet plants.
Do not save seed from infected fruit.
organic: Copper sprays can reduce spread when applied early.
Improve airflow and keep foliage dry.
chemical: Copper-based bactericides are the main option; follow the label.
Antibiotics are restricted in many countries; check local rules.
prevent: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants.
Mulch and stake plants to reduce splash.
tomato_bacterial_spot.escalate: If spots appear on fruit, contact an extension officer; marketability drops quickly.

tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.summary: Yellow leaf curl causes upward-curling, yellow-edged leaves and stunted plants. It is spread by whiteflies and has no cure.
act_now: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately.
Control whiteflies with sticky traps and approved products.
Do not take cuttings from infected plants.
organic: Yellow sticky traps and neem sprays for whitefly.
Use reflective mulch where available.
chemical: Use a registered insecticide for whitefly; rotate modes of action.
Spraying cannot cure infected plants.
prevent: Plant resistant varieties and use clean transplants.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.escalate: If more than 10% of plants are curling, remove them and alert your extension officer.

tomato_mosaic_virus.summary: Mosaic virus causes mottled light and dark green leaves, distortion, and stunting. It spreads by contact and contaminated seed.
act_now: Remove infected plants; do not compost.
Wash hands and disinfect tools after handling plants.
Avoid smoking near the crop; tobacco can carry the virus.
organic: No spray cures a virus; focus on hygiene and vector control.
Remove weeds and volunteer plants.
chemical: Insecticides may reduce aphid vectors but will not cure infected plants.
Do not save seed from infected plants.
tomato_mosaic_virus.escalate: If symptoms are widespread, contact an extension officer before replanting.

tomato_leaf_mold.summary: Leaf mould causes pale yellow patches on the upper leaf and olive-green mould underneath, usually in humid greenhouses.
act_now: Increase ventilation and reduce humidity.
Remove affected leaves and avoid overhead watering.
Space plants to dry faster.
organic: Copper or neem sprays can slow spread.
Keep foliage dry; water at the base in the morning.
chemical: Use a registered fungicide if humidity stays high and symptoms spread.
Rotate active ingredients.
prevent: Prune lower leaves and keep the canopy open.
tomato_leaf_mold.escalate: If mould covers most lower leaves, consult an extension officer.

tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.summary: Septoria causes small circular spots with grey centres and dark edges, starting on lower leaves.
act_now: Remove affected lower leaves and destroy them.
Mulch to stop soil splash.
Improve airflow by staking and pruning.
organic: Copper sprays can protect new growth.
Remove crop residue after harvest.
chemical: Use a registered fungicide if spots are moving up the canopy.
Rotate modes of action.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.escalate: If the upper canopy is affected, contact an extension officer.

tomato_early_blight.summary: Early blight causes brown concentric rings on older tomato leaves, often with a yellow halo.
act_now: Remove affected lower leaves and improve airflow.
Mulch and water at the base.
Keep plants vigorous; stress worsens the disease.
organic: Neem or copper sprays can slow progress.
Compost tea may support plant health.
chemical: Use a registered fungicide if lesions are moving upward.
Rotate active ingredients.
prevent: Stake plants and avoid overhead irrigation.
tomato_early_blight.escalate: If more than 30% of leaves are affected, consult an extension officer.

tomato_spider_mites_or_two_spotted_spide.summary: Spider mites cause fine yellow stippling and webbing on the underside of leaves. They thrive in hot, dry, dusty conditions.
act_now: Check the underside of leaves with a hand lens.
Spray the undersides with water to reduce dust and mites.
Remove heavily infested leaves.
organic: Insecticidal soap or neem oil, covering leaf undersides.
Encourage predatory mites; avoid broad-spectrum insecticides.
chemical: Use a registered acaricide only if webbing is widespread.
Rotate active ingredients; mites resist quickly.
prevent: Keep plants well watered and reduce dust.
Monitor weekly, especially in dry spells.
tomato_spider_mites_or_two_spotted_spide.escalate: If webbing covers growing tips, treat immediately and consult an extension officer.

tomato_target_spot.summary: Target spot causes brown lesions with concentric rings on leaves and fruit.
act_now: Remove affected leaves and fruit.
Improve airflow and avoid overhead watering.
Harvest fruit promptly.
organic: Copper or neem sprays can slow spread.
Mulch to reduce splash.
chemical: Use a registered fungicide if lesions are spreading.
Rotate modes of action.
tomato_target_spot.escalate: If fruit lesions are common, consult an extension officer.

apple_scab.summary: Apple scab causes olive-green to black velvety spots on leaves and fruit. It overwinters in fallen leaves.
act_now: Rake and destroy fallen leaves around the tree.
Prune to open the canopy.
Remove the worst affected fruit.
organic: Sulphur or copper sprays at bud break and early season, following the label.
Choose scab-resistant varieties for new plantings.
chemical: Use a registered scab fungicide from bud break through early summer.
Alternate active ingredients.
prevent: Clean up leaf litter every autumn.
apple_scab.escalate: If scab is severe every year, ask an extension officer about a spray schedule.

apple_black_rot.summary: Black rot causes brown rot on fruit and dark cankers on branches. It survives in dead wood and mummified fruit.
act_now: Remove mummified fruit and dead branches.
Prune out cankers with clean tools.
Destroy fallen fruit.
organic: Copper sprays during dormancy and early season.
Improve tree vigour and airflow.
chemical: Use a registered fungicide from bud break.
Rotate active ingredients.
apple_black_rot.escalate: If cankers are spreading on main limbs, consult an extension officer.

cedar_apple_rust.summary: Cedar apple rust causes bright orange spots on apple leaves and fruit. It needs juniper/cedar as an alternate host.
act_now: Remove galls from nearby juniper where practical.
Pick off severely affected leaves.
Improve airflow around trees.
organic: Sulphur sprays during the spring infection window.
Plant resistant apple varieties.
chemical: Registered fungicides from pink bud to early summer.
Follow local spray timing guidance.
prevent: Separate apples from juniper hosts where possible.
cedar_apple_rust.escalate: If fruit are heavily spotted, consult an extension officer.

cherry_powdery_mildew.summary: Powdery mildew causes white powdery patches on leaves and shoots, often in warm days and cool nights.
act_now: Prune out affected shoots and improve airflow.
Avoid excessive nitrogen.
Remove fallen leaves.
organic: Sulphur or potassium bicarbonate sprays, following the label.
Milk spray (1:9 with water) can reduce mild mildew.
chemical: Use a registered powdery-mildew fungicide if it is spreading.
Rotate modes of action.
cherry_powdery_mildew.escalate: If new shoots are covered, consult an extension officer.

grape_black_rot.summary: Grape black rot causes brown leaf spots and shrivelled black fruit. It overwinters in mummified berries.
act_now: Remove mummified berries and infected canes.
Open the canopy for airflow.
Destroy fallen debris.
organic: Copper or sulphur sprays from bud break, following the label.
Remove wild grapes nearby.
chemical: Registered fungicides from early bloom through fruit set.
Rotate active ingredients.
prevent: Prune and train vines for airflow.
grape_black_rot.escalate: If fruit loss is heavy, consult an extension officer.

grape_esca_black_measles.summary: Esca is a chronic wood disease causing tiger-stripe leaf symptoms and sudden vine decline. There is no cure.
act_now: Remove and destroy severely affected vines.
Prune late in dry weather and seal large cuts.
Do not propagate wood from affected vines.
organic: No curative spray exists; focus on vine hygiene.
Improve soil health and avoid drought stress.
chemical: Fungicides do not cure Esca; trunk-injection products are experimental and locally regulated.
Do not rely on sprays for control.
prevent: Avoid large pruning wounds in wet weather.
grape_esca_black_measles.escalate: If vines are dying suddenly, contact a viticulture extension officer.

grape_isariopsis_leaf_spot.summary: Isariopsis leaf spot causes dark angular spots on grape leaves, favoured by humid weather.
act_now: Remove affected leaves and improve airflow.
Avoid overhead irrigation.
Remove debris after harvest.
organic: Copper sprays can protect new growth.
Open the canopy.
chemical: Use a registered fungicide if spots are spreading.
Rotate modes of action.
grape_isariopsis_leaf_spot.escalate: If defoliation is significant, consult an extension officer.

orange_citrus_greening.summary: Citrus greening (HLB) causes blotchy mottled leaves, lopsided bitter fruit, and tree decline. It is spread by the Asian citrus psyllid and is incurable.
act_now: Report suspected greening to your local agriculture office; it is a regulated disease in many countries.
Remove and destroy confirmed infected trees.
Control psyllids with approved products and monitoring.
organic: Use yellow sticky traps to monitor psyllids.
Neem or horticultural oil can reduce psyllid pressure; it will not cure the tree.
chemical: Use a registered psyllid insecticide as part of an area-wide programme.
Do not move infected plant material.
prevent: Inspect new trees and control psyllids.
orange_citrus_greening.escalate: This is a reportable disease. Contact your national plant-protection office immediately.

peach_bacterial_spot.summary: Bacterial spot causes small dark spots on peach leaves and fruit, leading to defoliation and blemished fruit.
act_now: Remove infected leaves and fruit.
Avoid overhead irrigation and working in wet trees.
Disinfect tools.
organic: Copper sprays during dormancy and early season, following the label.
Improve airflow.
chemical: Copper is the main protectant; use label rates and avoid excessive use.
Antibiotics are restricted in many countries.
peach_bacterial_spot.escalate: If fruit blemishes are severe, consult an extension officer.

pepper_bacterial_spot.summary: Bacterial spot on pepper causes small water-soaked spots that turn brown on leaves and fruit.
act_now: Remove infected leaves and fruit.
Avoid overhead watering and handling wet plants.
Disinfect tools and hands.
organic: Copper sprays early in the season can slow spread.
Improve airflow and keep foliage dry.
chemical: Use a registered copper bactericide; follow the label.
Check local restrictions on antibiotic sprays.
prevent: Use certified clean seed and transplants.
pepper_bacterial_spot.escalate: If fruit are spotted, consult an extension officer; market value drops fast.

squash_powdery_mildew.summary: Powdery mildew coats squash leaves with white powder and reduces photosynthesis.
act_now: Remove the worst affected leaves.
Improve airflow and avoid overhead watering.
Keep plants well watered.
organic: Milk spray (1:9 with water) or potassium bicarbonate, following the label.
Sulphur sprays in cool weather.
chemical: Use a registered powdery-mildew fungicide if spread is rapid.
Rotate modes of action.
squash_powdery_mildew.escalate: If more than half the leaf area is white, consult an extension officer.

strawberry_leaf_scorch.summary: Leaf scorch causes purple to brown spots that merge, making leaves look scorched.
act_now: Remove affected leaves and old mulch.
Improve airflow and avoid overhead irrigation.
Renovate beds after harvest.
organic: Copper sprays after harvest and at renewal.
Use clean transplants.
chemical: Registered fungicides during wet periods.
Rotate active ingredients.
prevent: Use certified plants and resistant varieties.
Avoid dense beds and overhead water.
strawberry_leaf_scorch.escalate: If plants are weakening, consult an extension officer.
